title: Teaching coding agents idiomatic Rust with skills and clippy config
excerpt: A set of Agent Skills and a clippy config guide AI coders to write, review, and port idiomatic Rust across multiple models.
body:
A recent benchmark compared three agents that generated a tiny semver-parsing library. The version produced without any guidance exposed public fields, omitted error documentation, and used `unwrap()` in the example. After adding the BeautifulRust skills, the same agent emitted a struct with private fields, detailed `# Errors` docs, and a safe doctest that returns a `Result`. The contrast shows how a focused skill set can turn raw code generation into idiomatic Rust.

The BeautifulRust repository ships three Agent Skills, `rust-best-practices`, `rust-review`, and `rust-port`, plus a drop-in Clippy configuration. Together they teach coding agents to write, review, and port Rust that follows the official Rust API Guidelines, the Rust Design Patterns checklist, and a curated set of style rules. The following sections walk through each skill, show how they interact, and end with a concrete action you can take to make your own agents produce cleaner Rust.

## Rust best-practices skill for idiomatic code

The `rust-best-practices` skill loads whenever an agent writes or modifies Rust files. It nudges the generation toward the patterns recommended by the Rust API Guidelines and the Rust Design Patterns collection. For example, the skill enforces private fields for data structures unless public access is explicitly required, and it adds documentation blocks that list error conditions and provide `Result`-based doctests.

In the semver example, the skill transformed the struct from:

```rust
/// A semantic version. The fields are public for convenience.
pub struct Version {
    pub major: u64,
    pub minor: u64,
    pub patch: u64,
    pub pre: Vec<Identifier>,
    pub build: Vec<String>,
}
```

to the more idiomatic version:

```rust
/// A semantic version. Equality, hashing, and ordering ignore build metadata.
pub struct Version {
    major: u64,
    minor: u64,
    patch: u64,
    pre: Vec<Identifier>,
    build: Vec<String>,
}
```

The change hides the fields, clarifies the semantics of build metadata, and aligns the type with the “private fields, public getters” idiom that the Rust API Guidelines promote. The skill also injects a detailed `parse` method docstring that lists possible error cases, matching the style of the official `semver` crate.

Because the skill runs on every write, agents automatically inherit these conventions without needing a separate lint pass. The repository includes a `lints/` folder with a tested Clippy configuration that mirrors the same rules, so CI can enforce them as well.

## Rust review skill produces prioritized reports

When an existing codebase needs a health check, the `rust-review` skill examines a file, crate, or diff and emits a prioritized report. Each finding cites the specific rule it violates and offers a concrete fix. The report format is designed for machines, making it easy for CI pipelines or chat-ops bots to act on the suggestions.

A typical output might look like:

1. Private fields, Rule `rust_api_guidelines::private_fields`. Move `pub` off the struct fields and add accessor methods.  
2. Missing `# Errors` section, Rule `rust_design_patterns::error_doc`. Add an `# Errors` heading that enumerates all failure modes.  
3. Unsafe `unwrap()` in doctest, Rule `clippy::unwrap_used`. Replace with a `Result`-returning example.

The skill’s prioritization helps developers focus on the most impactful changes first. In the benchmark mentioned earlier, the review skill caught 29 of 30 checks on a library task, compared with only 24 of 30 when the agents lacked the skill. The extra coverage came from the skill’s ability to surface subtle documentation gaps and field-visibility issues that a raw LLM often overlooks.

## Rust port skill translates other languages to Rust

Porting code from C, C++, Python, Go, or JavaScript to Rust is a common source of bugs, especially when the original tests are not reproduced in the target language. The `rust-port` skill addresses this by first generating Rust tests that mirror the source language’s test suite. Only after those tests pass does the skill emit the translated implementation.

The skill re-uses the `rust-best-practices` skill for style and the `rust-review` skill for a final sanity check. This pipeline ensures that the ported code is not only functionally equivalent but also idiomatic. For instance, when porting a simple Python function that parses version strings, the skill produced a Rust module that uses the same error-handling strategy as the original Python code, but with private fields and proper `Result` types.

Because the skill works with multiple agents, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Gemini CLI, it can be dropped into existing workflows without changing the underlying model. The repository’s README explains that installing the skills is as simple as running:

```sh
npx skills add morganlinton/BeautifulRust
```

or, for Claude agents:

```sh
claude plugin install beautiful-
```

Both commands place the three skill folders (`rust-best-practices/`, `rust-review/`, `rust-port/`) where the agent looks for skills. The review and port skills lean on the best-practices skill for style, so installing all three provides a complete toolchain.

## The takeaway

The three BeautifulRust skills turn raw code generation into idiomatic Rust by enforcing best-practice patterns, delivering prioritized review reports, and guaranteeing behavior-preserving ports. Adding the `rust-best-practices` skill (and the accompanying Clippy config) to any supported agent gives immediate, machine-checkable improvements in field visibility, documentation, and error handling. Install the skills with a single command and let agents write Rust that the community already agrees is clean and maintainable.
